content.comment_body: I've prepared a step-by-step guide to manually install [product_name] on Linux distributions not based on SUSE or RHEL. This method works on Debian and its variants (including Linux Mint, Ubuntu), as well as on Arch Linux and related systems. # Thanks to [user_name] for advice on ethernet/wifi interfaces! This guide aims to help [product_name] users transitioning from Windows/Mac to GNU/Linux. Attached: [document]. The notes are available in English and Spanish. The guide is released under Creative Commons (CC-By), so feel free to share, translate, enhance, edit, and add new topics as needed. Contribute by testing the installation on other distributions (e.g., Gentoo, Slackware, Tiny Core Linux, Gobolinux, NixOS), and share your results in this forum thread. Best regards, [user_name]
Hello, [user_name]'s installation guide is excellent. I followed it for the latest Debian release and translated it into German. See [url] Best regards [user_name]

Thanks, I managed to get [product_name] [version_no] running on Kubuntu and Ubuntu Mate after using the provided installer. However, the settings window with the IP properties on the local PC did not open when clicking the gear icon initially. After performing the following steps: $ sudo mkdir /etc/sysconfig $ sudo mkdir /etc/sysconfig/network $ ifconfig (to find out your network adapter's name, e.g. enp2s0) $ sudo touch /etc/sysconfig/network/ifcfg-enp2s0 It started working; the settings window appears and program download is possible. It feels more straightforward to use compared to similar engineering platforms. However, [company_name] seems not to have implemented scalable fonts in their user interface. Available font scaling has been a standard in Windows/OSX/X11 for decades.

Hello, I installed [product_name] on Linux Mint 64-bit using the installer and encountered the Ethernet port issue mentioned earlier. The previous instructions solved it. I also created a launcher for [product_name]. Here are my installation notes: [product_name] installation: - Copy the CD contents to a temporary folder under ~/Downloads - Find .../CDROM_Installers/Disk1/InstData/Linux64/VM/Setup.bin - Change Setup.bin permissions in the file browser to "Allow executing file as program" or with terminal: sudo chmod 775 Setup.bin - In terminal: navigate to ~/CDROM_Installers/Disk1/InstData/Linux64/VM and run sudo ./Setup.bin Ethernet interface setup: - Create necessary directories under your root structure: $ cd /etc /etc$ sudo mkdir sysconfig /etc$ cd sysconfig /etc/sysconfig$ sudo mkdir network /etc/sysconfig$ cd network /etc/sysconfig/network$ ifconfig (get the adapter name) /etc/sysconfig/network$ sudo touch ifcfg-enp2s0 I used the disk installer with sudo. Everything installed and [product_name] is functional. However, I can only launch [product_name] Web Editor as a superuser (using sudo in terminal). I have not been able to create a launcher button for normal user execution, as the software only runs as root. Not being very experienced with Linux permissions, I would appreciate guidance on file permission changes needed for normal user launching. Any help welcome! Thanks, [user_name]

If you're the only regular user on your machine, try running this from the command line: sudo chown -R <yourusername>.<yourgroupname> </directory_where_[product_name]_Web_Editor_installed> For example: sudo chown -R wwmo.wwmo /usr/local/lib/[product_name]_Web_Editor
Hi, thanks. I used the disk installer with sudo to complete the installation. What command did you use specifically?

analysis.insight_summary: Community members are successfully installing [product_name] on a wide variety of Linux distributions beyond the officially supported ones, utilizing comprehensive guides and troubleshooting advice. The main usability obstacles are initial Ethernet network interface setup and challenges running associated tools (notably [product_name] Web Editor) as non-superusers due to file permission constraints. Another common complaint is the lack of adjustable font scaling in the user interface, affecting ease of use on modern displays.
analysis.user_expectations: Users expect [product_name] and related tools to install and function smoothly across major Linux distributions, support graphical interface launching as regular users, recognize network adapters effortlessly, and offer a more user-friendly UI with scalable fonts.
